clue.text: Diminutive Americans certainly have the pull

definitions.meaning: a short, informal name for people from the United States, clipped from Yankees
the verb for tugging sharply, so the word for 'jerks hard' certainly has pull in it

explanation.surface: Short Americans manage to exert influence after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Clipped Yankees are Americans in slang, and to jerk something toward you is to tug, or pull, it.

clue.text: They are happiest when they get the wind up.

definitions.text: They are happiest when they get the wind up.

parts.words: They are happiest when they get the wind up.
parts.note: to get the wind up is to be frightened, but read literally it means the breeze rising, which sailors welcome

explanation.surface: Some people only enjoy themselves when scared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the wind up' is British slang for becoming nervous; the sailors here want a rising breeze to fill their sails.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors of pleasure boats need a good breeze to sail, so a rising wind delights them.

clue.text: Date in Rome when one goes in opposite directions

indicators.note: one is placed in the middle of the pair of compass points, so one word is enclosed by the other

parts.note: north and south are opposite compass directions, N and S
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman feast day when people scatter in all directions.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar this was the ninth day before the Ides, falling on the 5th or 7th of a month.

clue.text: Action 'of a man of-straw

parts.note: a man of straw is a feeble person, but here it is someone sipping a drink through a straw and drawing it up

explanation.surface: What a weak, ineffectual person does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of straw' is an idiom for a person of no substance; here it is a drinker using a straw.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing liquid up a straw works by lowering pressure in the mouth, so the drinker's action is sucking.

clue.text: He's usually got something to shout about

definitions.text: He's usually got something to shout about

parts.words: He's usually got something to shout about
parts.note: read literally: a man whose job is to call out public announcements in the streets

explanation.surface: Someone with good news always has cause to celebrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something to shout about' is an idiom for a reason to boast; here it is meant literally, the news a town official bellowed in the square.
explanation.definitionFit: A town's bellman walked the streets calling out proclamations, so shouting news was the whole job.

clue.text: They are less by far than our old currency

indicators.note: the word far is taken away from the old coin, as less means minus

parts.note: the farthing was an old British coin worth a quarter of a penny
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some items are worth even less than an old copper coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less by far' reads as 'much smaller'; it is the instruction to take FAR off. A FARTHING was the smallest pre-decimal British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun 'they' stands for unspecified objects, and the plural noun names objects in general.

clue.text: Terrier on guard duty ?

parts.note: a small dog set to keep watch over a house, the general term also used for any vigilant monitoring body

explanation.surface: A small dog keeps sentry over the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Any dog posted to guard property takes this name, and a terrier is one example, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog kept to guard premises and bark at intruders is a guard dog, and a terrier can serve as one.

clue.text: Opportunity at the beginning of life in the Church

definitions.note: the definition names where the answer is found, a part of a church building, so it is a noun for a place

parts.note: a chance is an opportunity

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word life is used

explanation.surface: A chance to start life within the church, perhaps by baptism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the beginning of life' looks like a christening; it only takes L, the first letter of 'life'.
explanation.definitionFit: The area of a church near the altar, reserved for clergy and choir, is found inside the church building.

clue.text: Unemployed at Hatch End ?

parts.note: Hatch End is a London suburb, but read as hatching, the device used for hatching eggs is not idle but in use there

explanation.surface: Someone out of work in the London suburb of Hatch End.
explanation.walkthrough: Hatch End is a district of north-west London; read literally, it is the business end of hatching eggs, where this machine is busy, so 'Unemployed' is the contrast the question mark marks.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated cabinet keeps eggs warm until the chicks hatch out.

clue.text: The one to give you a lift -in a helicopter

definitions.text: The one to give you a lift -in a helicopter

parts.words: The one to give you a lift -in a helicopter
parts.note: a lift is usually a ride offered by a friend; here it is the upward force produced by the spinning blades on top of a helicopter

explanation.surface: A friend who will give you a ride, and in a helicopter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give you a lift' suggests a kind driver; it is the aerodynamic lift of the helicopter's blades.
explanation.definitionFit: A helicopter's spinning blade assembly generates the upward force that raises the craft off the ground.

clue.text: He seems to study his part under compulsion

definitions.text: He seems to study his part under compulsion

parts.note: to con is an old verb for studying or learning by heart
an actor's part is written in his script

explanation.surface: An actor learns his lines only because he has been made to.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: someone drafted by compulsion, who in the wordplay pores over (cons) his lines (script).
explanation.definitionFit: A draftee is a man enlisted into the forces by legal compulsion rather than volunteering.

clue.text: A Northerner takes a course

parts.note: a Scot lives in the north of Britain

explanation.surface: A man from up north enrols on a course of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes a course' suggests education; the course is a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a famous English racecourse in Berkshire, home of Royal Ascot.

clue.text: One-man trunk-moving business

parts.note: the trunk is a tree trunk, heaved end over end by a single strong man at a Highland games, not luggage shifted by a removals firm

explanation.surface: A small removals firm run by one man to carry luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a Scottish Highland games event in which one competitor throws a long pole made from a tree trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland event has one athlete hurl a huge wooden pole, a trimmed tree trunk, so it flips end over end.

clue.text: Time may be short, but it is of some importance

definitions.meaning: significant, so the noun here is weight or consequence

explanation.surface: Life may be brief, but it still matters.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a very brief instant and, in 'of great moment', significance or weight.

clue.text: Lent the day after in France

definitions.text: Lent the day after in France

parts.words: Lent the day after in France
parts.note: Lent begins the day after a French-named feast, Shrove Tuesday, famous for carnival

explanation.surface: Something was loaned the following day in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lent' reads as 'loaned'; it is the Christian fast, which begins the day after Shrove Tuesday, called by its French name.
explanation.definitionFit: The carnival day before Ash Wednesday has the French name meaning Fat Tuesday, and Lent follows next day.

clue.text: Bad language used by 5?

parts.note: 5 is the guard dog of 5-down, so its speech is a canine kind of Latin, the term for corrupt or mangled Latin

explanation.surface: A guard dog swears at intruders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad language' suggests swearing; it is debased Latin, named after the dog of 5-down. The grid's printed BOG LATIN is the B/D misread of the solution page; the first letter is unchecked.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog Latin is a mock or badly made Latin, a corrupt imitation of the classical tongue.

clue.text: Any recess may be unavoidable

indicators.note: the letters of the two words may be rearranged into a different word

explanation.surface: Any holiday break may be compulsory.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unavoidable is needed or inevitable, a synonym for essential or required.

clue.text: Proverbially not a gift of the gods

definitions.text: Proverbially not a gift of the gods

parts.words: Proverbially not a gift of the gods
parts.note: the proverb 'whom the gods love die young' implies that those the gods favour are not granted many years

explanation.surface: A saying that some blessing does not come from heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'whom the gods love die young' means the gods' favourites die early, so length of years is not what they give.
explanation.definitionFit: Living to a great age is denied the gods' favourites, according to the old proverb.

clue.text: He's a regular tell-tale

parts.note: a tell-tale is usually a sneak, but here it is someone who tells a tale as a matter of course

explanation.surface: He constantly snitches on others.
explanation.walkthrough: A tell-tale is a schoolchild who sneaks on friends; split, it is one who tells the tale of a story.
explanation.definitionFit: The voice who relates a story's events is its storyteller, telling the tale throughout.

clue.text: I put an end to an advertisement for stout

indicators.note: I and the word for put are joined at the end of the word for an advertisement

parts.note: ad is short for an advertisement
to pose, as in to pose a question, is to put it

explanation.surface: Someone stops a beer commercial from running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put an end to' looks like 'stop'; it says I and POSE go at the end of AD. 'Stout' looks like the beer but is the adjective for fat.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means fatty, and a stout person carries plenty of fat.

clue.text: Such old Greek singers bring gold into style

indicators.note: gold is brought into the middle of the word for style, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: chic means stylishness
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Ancient Greek performers add glitter to their fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to a chorus, such as the chanting groups of ancient Greek drama.

clue.text: Asinine utterances

parts.note: asinine usually means foolish, but here it means belonging to an ass, so the noises a donkey makes

explanation.surface: Stupid remarks made by a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asinine' usually means silly; here it is literal, 'of an ass', so the braying a donkey makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey's bray is imitated in English as a two-part sound, and these are its cries.

clue.text: Such industrious people here

indicators.note: the people are here, inside the words Such industrious, spanning the join

explanation.surface: Hard-working people of that kind live in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' points into 'Such industrious', where the answer runs across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of the main religion of India form a religious people.

clue.text: Prerequisites for the running of some going concerns

definitions.text: Prerequisites for the running of some going concerns

parts.words: Prerequisites for the running of some going concerns
parts.note: a going concern is a business, but here it is something that literally goes on the road, a car, which needs a legal permit to be run

explanation.surface: What is needed before a profitable business can be managed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going concern' is a business trading profitably; here it is read as a vehicle in motion, and the 'running' is driving it.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorists must hold official permits before they may legally take a car out on public roads.

clue.text: Aristocratic description of the French state

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'
Cal is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: How the French nobility might describe the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French state' reads as France; it is DU (French 'of the') plus CAL (California).
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to a duke, one of the highest ranks of nobility.

clue.text: Make provision for these old cousins?

definitions.meaning: to supply food or other needs for someone
...-cousins is an old phrase for close friends, so these are the old kind of cousins

explanation.surface: Should we provide for these elderly relatives?
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to supply food or needs, and old English had cater-cousins for intimate friends.

clue.text: Shakespearian character in the antique shop

definitions.meaning: A gentleman attending Duke Orsino in Twelfth Night
an object of the kind found in an antique shop: a rare or quaint collectable

explanation.surface: A figure from Shakespeare's plays turns up in an antique shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Orsino's attendant in Twelfth Night bears this name, and the word also means an unusual collectable object or bibelot.

clue.text: Refreshing start of a Calcutta hole? Sound idea

indicators.note: the idea is to be heard, so the phrase for the golf peg is said and another spelling written

parts.note: a golf hole starts at the tee, and one in Calcutta would be an Indian tee

explanation.surface: An Indian golf course offers a drink before play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calcutta hole' calls up the Black Hole of Calcutta, but the hole is a golfing one; a hole begins at the tee, so an Indian tee. 'Refreshing' stands for a refreshing drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A cup of Assam or Darjeeling from the subcontinent is a classic restorative drink.

clue.text: What Mark Antony wanted his friends to be

definitions.text: What Mark Antony wanted his friends to be

parts.words: What Mark Antony wanted his friends to be
parts.note: his funeral speech in Julius Caesar opens 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears'

explanation.surface: Antony hoped his companions would stay loyal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar Antony asks his friends to lend him their ears, so he wants them to pay attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Lending one's ears means paying attention, so those he addressed were to become his audience.

clue.text: Roses perhaps flung by the breakers

definitions.meaning: a small bunch of flowers on one stem or in a posy, roses being an example
breakers are waves, which throw fine drops of seawater into the air

explanation.surface: Roses are hurled about by vandals.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a sprig of flowers such as roses and the fine mist thrown up when waves crash.
